12 OctFell 1.11% to 259.53 after Cantor Fitzgerald cut its target to $310 from $320, Overweight maintained, on volume about 47% below its 46.5m average.
1 SepThe litigation to keep in view: the FTC and 22 state attorneys general sued over sponsored-product ad auctions. The complaint alleges Amazon changed the auction rules in 2019 and interfered in as many as 80% of sponsored-product auctions, extracting more than $20bn from over a million sellers. Advertising is $19.8bn a quarter, up 26%. Amazon says winning bids fell 50% between 2019 and 2025 and the system saved advertisers about $8bn.

Street: Strong Buy · 60 analysts, average target $331.20 — 30.0% above the 254.76 close.

Two hot prints in two days, and the long end fell through both of them

1. The retail sales control group is the most important number nobody led with. Headline retail sales rose 0.8% against 0.3% expected, to $745.0bn, up 6.3% on the year, with August revised up. Read alone it describes a strong consumer and argues for a hike. But the control group rose 0.1% against 0.3% expected, after +1.2% in August, and excluding petrol stations the increase was 0.2%. Set that beside a CPI in which gasoline did over half the monthly increase and a PPI in which gasoline rose 20.3% at the producer level and energy goods 10.8%, and the three releases say one thing: money is moving into the fuel tank and out of everything else. A consumer spending more on petrol and the same on everything else is not an inflating economy. It is a squeezed one.

2. Which is why a PPI at nearly three times forecast produced a twelve-basis-point rally in the long end. 1.3% against 0.5% is an enormous miss, and the ten-year fell to roughly 5.07% and the thirty-year to 5.41%, a three-week low. Hike odds for 28 October fell from about 50% to roughly 27%. The bond market has now, in five consecutive sessions, declined to price the inflation it was handed: through a thirty-year auction, a flattening, a quiet Tuesday, a hot CPI and a hot PPI, the thirty-year has gone from 5.67% to 5.41%. The term-premium and supply story cannot explain the spike to 5.33% on Wednesday; the inflation story cannot explain any of the five closes. What explains both is a market that reads energy-driven price rises as demand destruction — and buys duration into it.

3. The equity market split along exactly that line, and this book is on the wrong side of it. The Russell rose 1.38% and the Dow 1.08% — the two most rate-sensitive, most domestically cyclical indices, both up hard on the day the hike was priced out. The Nasdaq managed 0.08% and the S&P 0.33%. Over the full week the Dow is the only index up, at +1%, while the Nasdaq is down 2.4% and the Russell 1.4%. So the rotation that this brief has tracked since 6 October did not pause on Thursday — it completed. A book of long-duration growth names made money when rates fell and lost more when they rose, and finished the week behind an index of companies that sell things now. That is a factor exposure, not a stock-picking outcome, and no stop placement addresses it.

The two benchmarks split three dollars apart in a single session

WTI settled $97.97, up $2.88 or 3.03%, on a sharp decline in US crude inventories. Brent settled $105.92, down 14 cents, as traders weighed a possible United States easing of restrictions on the 'shadow fleet' of tankers — the vessels moving sanctioned crude — against the standing Middle East premium. The spread between the two collapsed to $7.95 from $10.97, a three-dollar narrowing in one day and the tightest it has been in this stretch.

That split is worth more attention than either number alone. An American inventory draw tightening WTI while a prospective sanctions easing loosens Brent is the two halves of the oil market being priced by different news for the first time since the conflict began. If the shadow-fleet easing is real it puts sanctioned barrels into the seaborne market, which is Brent's problem and not WTI's. If the US draw persists, the American barrel keeps tightening into a refining system that is already the constraint.

And the refining constraint is the part that reaches this book. The IEA's figure from Wednesday still stands: combined net gasoil exports from the Middle East and Russia fell 1.3m barrels a day in September to 820,000, down more than 60% year on year, with no stock rebuild expected before the second half of 2027. Gulf crude exports are back at 13.9m barrels a day, over 75% of pre-war, while refined product exports are 1.9m against 4.7m before the war. Crude flows; product does not. That gap is why gasoline rose 20.3% at the producer level in September and did over half of the CPI increase — and why it then showed up as a retail-sales beat that was really a fuel bill.

So the war is now the transmission mechanism and not the headline. Nothing was struck on Thursday. The missile that hit Aramco's Dhahran command centre on Tuesday moved crude about a dollar. What moves this book is the second-order effect: energy into the price indices, price indices into the rate expectation, rate expectation into the multiple on three long-duration growth names. Crude at $97.97 is three dollars higher than when the week began, and the October CPI lands 10 November with that embedded in it.

Friday is the first thing in three weeks that produces evidence rather than sourcing. iPhone Duo pre-orders open at 5am Pacific, with sale on the 23rd at $1,999 for 256GB rising to $3,199 for 2TB, and 28 further countries on the 30th. Three parties now disagree about iPhone 18 demand and all three are working from supply-chain contacts: Nikkei says Pro production is being cut; Securities Times says Pro supply targets are unchanged and Duo orders were raised 30% toward 10 million units; Bank of America, Buy at $370, reports Pro delivery times shorter than a year ago. Then the Fed on the 28th, into a market that has changed its mind twice in three days. Hike odds for that meeting went from about 22% before Wednesday's CPI, to about 50% after it, to roughly 27% after Thursday's PPI and retail sales. A December hike was priced near 88% earlier in the week. The useful question is not which way the Fed goes but whether the long end keeps falling regardless — five sessions now, through everything the data has thrown at it. If it does, the rate-sensitive end of the market keeps winning and this book keeps lagging it. If the long end turns, every multiple here reprices upward and the week just gone was noise.

Three things to watch in this book. Whether AMZN, at +5.88R and 66% of the open profit, keeps carrying the book — it rose on Thursday while the rest fell, which is concentration working, and the gain is still entirely unprotected. Whether PLTR holds above +0.8R, because three hundredths of an R below that the breakeven question is dropped for good. And whether OKTA stabilises after 10.2% in three sessions on no company news. All three are the same question asked three ways: does the long end keep falling.

The standing position: do nothing. Heat is 3.00R at a 3.0R cap, all 4 holdings are green, the nearest stop that can take capital is 11.6% away on Thursday's low, and nothing can be added. Three index records were set this week and the only index that fell was the one measuring the median company. The Russell lost 0.91% — 2.12σ, the largest reading on the board — while the S&P rose 1.15% at 1.69σ, the Dow 0.93% and the Nasdaq 0.64% at 1.01σ. In point terms: S&P +88.82, Dow +477.99, Nasdaq +175.31, Russell −25.91. A record-setting week in which small caps fell is not a rally with poor breadth; it is two different markets, and this is the third consecutive week the gap has widened.

The rotation inverted, and the week is the evidence. The Dow beat the Nasdaq over the five sessions — 0.93% against 0.64% — after a quarter in which the Nasdaq beat the Dow by more than five points. The Dow led on three of the last four sessions. That is not a one-day funding effect any more. For a book holding three long-duration growth names and nothing on the other side, it is the single most relevant structural fact of the week, and it sits oddly beside the book's own result.

The rate story turned two-sided for the first time. Monday through Wednesday it ran exactly as it had for a fortnight: ISM services prices paid up 1.4 to 74.0 against 72.9 expected, a second month above 72, while employment sat at 50.1; the two-year falling on the weak half and the ten-year making 52-week highs at 5.315% and touching 5.35% intraday, the thirty-year at 5.670%. Wednesday added the global framing — France's index down 1.2% amid mass budget protests, debt heading for 121.7% of GDP in 2027, and projected interest payments of €74.5bn exceeding what the country spends on education. The IMF's Georgieva cited record public debt; Ray Dalio warned about America's.

Then it stopped behaving. Thursday the long end eased through a thirty-year auction — the first direct test of the supply argument, and the ten-year closed near 5.24%, its lowest in a week. Friday the curve flattened: the two-year rose 3.9 basis points to 4.795% while the thirty-year sat flat at 5.608%, and it did so on a Michigan sentiment print that fell to 46.3 from 48.1 against 47.6 expected. Two consecutive sessions now fail to fit the term-premium story after five that fitted it exactly. It is not refuted — the thirty-year is still near a 24-year high and the September Fed minutes promise another hike this year — but this is the first sustained counter-evidence, and CPI on Tuesday decides it.

And the week ended with a structural repricing nobody had on the calendar. A reported $8bn SpaceX purchase of 800 MHz spectrum for Starlink Mobile took 12.26% out of T-Mobile on Friday and about 10.9% each out of Verizon and AT&T, while Crown Castle rose 11.27% and the other tower owners with it. Communication Services closed the week's worst sector. Crude went almost nowhere across five sessions — $91.11 to $90.76 — having been $87.77 on Tuesday and almost $93 on Thursday. Gold rose 0.83% to $4,174.68, its first weekly gain in three.

The largest weekly gain in three weeks, and two positions through +1R

Nothing was opened, closed, trimmed or moved. Checked against the lowest low of all five sessions rather than any close, the nearest any holding came to a stop was AAPL at 8.66%, on Monday's 330.62. No stop was in question at any point.

The book gained $43.89 on the week and now carries +88.68 open at +4.42R — the best mark it has held. 2 of the 3 positions are above +1R, against none a fortnight ago. Friday did most of it, and on broker notes rather than company news. OKTA rose 5.41% to 232.13, a new 52-week high, on BMO Capital's move to $245 from $230 with Outperform maintained. PLTR rose 5.17% to 209.05, an all-time closing high past the $208.88 record of 3 November last year, on Goldman's upgrade to Buy from Neutral with a $230 target and Barclays initiating at Overweight with $265. Goldman's case was sovereign AI, bespoke applications, a verticalisation strategy and a head start on agents; Barclays cited deep competitive moats. Neither company said anything. That is worth stating plainly: two positions re-rated five percent in a session because analysts changed their minds, and moves made that way unwind as easily as they arrive.

PLTR rose 10.75% across the week, the best performance in either book. From 188.75 to 209.05, and the shape matters: three sessions of reaching above 192 and closing below 190 early in the week, then three consecutive held gains, then Friday's all-time high. The position has gone from +0.25R on Monday to +1.23R. On no company news at any point — the move is Goldman, Barclays and Dan Ives putting it in his top five tech picks for 2027. The 2 November print is expected to show whether US commercial revenue has overtaken government; in Q2 commercial grew 149% to $764m against government's 90% to $809m.

AAPL was the week's laggard and the only holding with bad news of its own. Up 0.88% over the five sessions, which flatters it: it drifted between 330 and 334 for four days while the S&P made a record, cleared the 338.40 pre-Ternus level on Thursday for the first time since the 29 September fall, and then gave it straight back on Friday — down 1.11%, and about 2.2% premarket, on a report of iPhone 18 Pro component order cuts, with Skyworks down 6.41% on the same story. Eight sessions to recover nine dollars and one to lose four of them. Order-cut reports are a supply-chain read and are frequently wrong, but they are the first hard, checkable claim about the cycle, and the answer comes on 29 October.

What the week leaves behind. Heat at the cap, so nothing can be added. Every holding green, with OKTA at +2.46R and no stop closer than 8.7% on the week's lowest low. Two positions past the +1R threshold where a breakeven stop becomes arithmetically interesting — both flagged in the dailies, neither urgent. And a result that is entirely unrealised, in a book that has not been touched in twenty-two sessions. The honest summary of the week is that it was the best one in two months and that nothing in it was earned by a decision.

The rate thesis acquired its first counter-evidence, and the rotation inverted

1. Two sessions broke the pattern that five had built. From 29 September the long end rose on data that argued for lower yields four times in five sessions — a twelve-year low in consumer confidence, a downside core PCE miss at 3.0% against 3.3%, payrolls at 29,000 against 90,000 with 60,000 revised out, and Monday's ISM services. By Wednesday the thirty-year was at 5.671% and the ten-year had touched 5.35%, its highest since 2002, with the framing turning global. Then Thursday the long end eased through a thirty-year auction, and Friday the curve flattened on a weak sentiment print. An auction is where a supply thesis is actually tested, and that one did not go badly. This brief has published the supply argument for a fortnight; it is recording the counter-evidence with the same weight.

2. The index records and the median stock are describing different economies. The S&P set its first record since 13 August on Tuesday with genuinely broad internals — ten of eleven sectors, the equal-weight index matching the cap-weighted one, positive volume at 65.1% of NYSE turnover — and still only 24 new 52-week highs, with the McClellan Summation negative. By Friday the week showed the S&P up 1.2% and the Russell down 0.9%, and Michigan consumer sentiment had fallen to 46.3. Three records in a week when small caps fell and the consumer reached a multi-decade low of confidence is a market carried by its largest weights. This book owns three of those weights, which is why it had its largest weekly gain in three weeks.

3. The AI trade showed its first crack, and it was about funding. Thursday the Nasdaq fell 1.25% on a semiconductor sell-off while the Dow rose and most S&P constituents were higher — the first session in this run where the AI complex moved alone. The trigger was an Nvidia-backed Australian data-centre company failing to raise the support it had sought: a question about the capital behind capacity rather than about demand for compute, and the more dangerous of the two, because capacity already contracted has to be paid for regardless. Alphabet carries $195-205bn of guided capex and, since Tuesday, a twenty-year obligation for 3.6 gigawatts of power. It was the only holding to fall that day. By Friday the market had moved on; the question has not been answered.

The week the war stopped setting the price of oil

Crude ended the week where it started. WTI went $91.11 to $90.76, a move of less than four tenths of a percent across five sessions that contained a hurricane, a tanker attack and a presidential commitment on military timing. The range inside that was wide — $87.77 on Tuesday, almost $93 on Thursday — and Brent finished $103.35. A price that round-trips through that much news is a price that has stopped taking its direction from the conflict.

The most consequential thing said was about the calendar. On Thursday Trump said the United States will not attack Iran before the November midterm elections, citing productive diplomacy. It is the first dated commitment on timing since the conflict began and it removes, for roughly four weeks, the tail the oil price had been intermittently pricing. Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz happened the same day. Washington's reply to Tehran's seven-point proposal reached the cabinet through Qatari mediation on 30 September and neither side has disclosed its contents since.

What moved the price was weather and Saudi pricing. Hurricane Isaias shut in about a quarter of Gulf of Mexico output mid-week, with Chevron, Shell and BP evacuating platforms and Shell pulling off six; the premium came out on Friday as the path clarified. Against that, OPEC+ held quotas at the previous weekend and Saudi Arabia cut Arab Light for Asian buyers to $5 below benchmark, a six-year low, from a $2 discount, to take share as Gulf flows recovered. Kpler had regional exports above pre-conflict levels on 14 days in September, with a seven-day average of 18.3m barrels a day on the 30th.

And the man selling the oil spent Monday explaining that there is none spare. Aramco's Amin Nasser, at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London, called global stockpiles scarily thin: under 6 billion barrels of commercial inventory against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, less than 10% practically available, around 3 billion barrels of supply lost and over a billion drawn to cover it, with rebuilding at up to two years even after Hormuz fully reopens and an extra 2 million barrels a day needed for eighteen months. The flow has recovered and the buffer has not. That is why a storm moved crude 2.7% on Wednesday, and it is the asymmetry this book carries without being positioned for it.

One print, and a fortnight of argument riding on it

September CPI on Tuesday has to settle three things at once. Whether the ISM prices indices at 77.9 in manufacturing and 74.0 in services are feeding through, when core PCE missed at 3.0% against 3.3% a fortnight ago. Whether the Fed's minutes and Waller's more hikes will likely be needed describe a committee that will act or one that is talking. And whether the long end is an inflation trade or a supply one — because Thursday's auction and Friday's flattening are the first two pieces of evidence for the second reading being wrong, and a hot print removes them.

Then nothing from the companies for a fortnight. Alphabet reports 28 October on the same day the Fed decides, Apple the 29th, Palantir 2 November, Okta in early December. Three of this book's holdings report inside five sessions at the end of the month, immediately after a rate decision. Apple's print now has an order-cut report to answer, and Alphabet's lands into a funding scare rather than an enthusiasm.

Three things to watch through the gap. Whether the broker-driven re-ratings hold: two positions in this book gained more than five percent on upgrades alone, with nothing from either company, and that is the least durable kind of gain there is. Whether the Dow keeps beating the Nasdaq — it did over a full week and on three of four sessions, and this book owns nothing on that side. And whether the Russell can stop falling: down 0.9% in a week the S&P gained 1.2% is the clearest available statement that the records are not describing the median company.

The standing discipline. Heat is 3.00R against a 3.0R cap, so nothing on the screener is actionable whatever it returns. All 3 holdings are green, the nearest any came to a stop in five sessions was 8.7% on the week's lowest low, and 2 of them now sit above +1R. Twenty-two sessions without a change — the sixth consecutive week in which the right decision was made by not being made, and the first in which that produced a result worth having.

The stop was 251.84. The open was 250.89. There was no trade in between. Amazon gapped down more than three dollars from Wednesday's close, so a stop at the fill could not fill at the fill — it filled at the open, 95 cents lower, and the position realises −2.85, or −0.14R, instead of nothing. It then fell to 248.65 and recovered six dollars to close 254.76, up 0.27% on the day and above the stop. So the sequence was: taken out near the low of a reversal day, on no company news, in a position that finished the session higher than it started it.

What it cost and what it did not. The realised figure is −2.85 on $755.52 of committed capital, which is −0.38% — call it a flat trade with slippage. Eight sessions of exposure for a third of a percent of the stake. The part that matters more is what did not happen: heat is unchanged at 3.05R. A stop sitting at the entry was carrying no risk at all, so closing the position freed nothing, and this book is still at its cap and still cannot add a position. The lesson the week actually taught is narrower than it looks: a breakeven stop protects capital and guarantees nothing about the fill, and in a $250 stock that gaps three dollars overnight, 'riskless' meant 'risk of about a dollar a share'.

What is left is three positions inside a third of an R of each other. GOOG at +0.94R, AAPL at +0.97R, OKTA at +1.28R — an R-spread of 0.34R, the narrowest this book has been. Only OKTA is above +1R. The book carries +64.87 open at +3.19R and +62.02 for the quarter against +74.69 of open profit on Wednesday; across the week it is -55.82. Three names, one factor pricing all of them, and no capacity to add: that is the position to sit in until something changes.

OKTA fell again but the low is the number to look at. It opened at 204.14, fell to 202.97 and closed 208.52, down 1.60% — -3.40 on the day. At that low the position was +1.01R, having been +2.46R a week ago. From Friday's 232.13 it is down 10.2% across three sessions, on no company news at all. It is still +1.28R and 14.1% above the fill, with the stop 19.9% below Thursday's low. It is the largest single share of the open profit at 40%. A stock that can lose ten percent of its price and nearly half its R in three sessions is not being valued on anything the company does; it is being valued on the discount rate, and this week the discount rate changed its mind twice.

AAPL was the only holding that did not bounce, and the timing is awkward. It opened at 346.95, close to the 347.85 high, and drifted down all session to close 342.00, two cents off its low — the exact mirror of Wednesday, when it was the only thing that rose. At +0.97R it has slipped back below the threshold it crossed on Wednesday. No company news on the day. What makes it awkward is the calendar: the iPhone Duo opens for pre-order on Friday at 5am Pacific, and the stock spent the session before it being sold. Against that, the evidence is genuinely split — Securities Times has Duo orders raised 30% toward 10 million units and the iPhone 18 Pro supply target unchanged; Nikkei has Pro production being cut on weak demand; Bank of America holds Buy at $370 while reporting shorter Pro delivery times than a year ago. Friday answers it with numbers rather than sourcing.

GOOG is +0.94R, below the threshold, and it was the best thing in the book on the day. It opened at 340.53, fell to 336.82 — its lowest since 6 October — and closed 344.91, up 0.37%, recovering the whole of an eight-dollar range. The stop question stays off the table below +1R. 3. The equity market split along exactly that line, and this book is on the wrong side of it. The Russell rose 1.38% and the Dow 1.08% — the two most rate-sensitive, most domestically cyclical indices, both up hard on the day the hike was priced out. The Nasdaq managed 0.08% and the S&P 0.33%. Over the full week the Dow is the only index up, at +1%, while the Nasdaq is down 2.4% and the Russell 1.4%. So the rotation that this brief has tracked since 6 October did not pause on Thursday — it completed. A book of long-duration growth names made money when rates fell and lost more when they rose, and finished the week behind an index of companies that sell things now. That is a factor exposure, not a stock-picking outcome, and no stop placement addresses it.

The two benchmarks split three dollars apart in a single session

WTI settled $97.97, up $2.88 or 3.03%, on a sharp decline in US crude inventories. Brent settled $105.92, down 14 cents, as traders weighed a possible United States easing of restrictions on the 'shadow fleet' of tankers — the vessels moving sanctioned crude — against the standing Middle East premium. The spread between the two collapsed to $7.95 from $10.97, a three-dollar narrowing in one day and the tightest it has been in this stretch.

That split is worth more attention than either number alone. An American inventory draw tightening WTI while a prospective sanctions easing loosens Brent is the two halves of the oil market being priced by different news for the first time since the conflict began. If the shadow-fleet easing is real it puts sanctioned barrels into the seaborne market, which is Brent's problem and not WTI's. If the US draw persists, the American barrel keeps tightening into a refining system that is already the constraint.

And the refining constraint is the part that reaches this book. The IEA's figure from Wednesday still stands: combined net gasoil exports from the Middle East and Russia fell 1.3m barrels a day in September to 820,000, down more than 60% year on year, with no stock rebuild expected before the second half of 2027. Gulf crude exports are back at 13.9m barrels a day, over 75% of pre-war, while refined product exports are 1.9m against 4.7m before the war. Crude flows; product does not. That gap is why gasoline rose 20.3% at the producer level in September and did over half of the CPI increase — and why it then showed up as a retail-sales beat that was really a fuel bill.

So the war is now the transmission mechanism and not the headline. Nothing was struck on Thursday. The missile that hit Aramco's Dhahran command centre on Tuesday moved crude about a dollar. What moves this book is the second-order effect: energy into the price indices, price indices into the rate expectation, rate expectation into the multiple on three long-duration growth names. Crude at $97.97 is three dollars higher than when the week began, and the October CPI lands 10 November with that embedded in it.

weekly.headline: Three records, and the only index that fell was the one measuring the median company — while the rate thesis found its first counter-evidence
weekly.standfirst: The S&P set its first record close since 13 August on Tuesday and came within a whisker of it again on Friday, closing the week +1.2% with the Dow +0.9% and the Nasdaq +0.6% — and the Russell down 0.9%, the largest move on the board. The Dow beat the Nasdaq over five sessions for the first time since the quarter turned. Underneath, the long end made 52-week highs through Wednesday, touching 5.35% on the ten-year and 5.671% on the thirty, with the pressure turning global — France’s index down 1.2% on a budget whose €74.5bn interest bill exceeds its education spending — and the Fed’s minutes promising another hike. Then it eased through a thirty-year auction on Thursday and flattened on Friday, the first counter-evidence in a fortnight. In the book nothing was opened, closed or moved for a sixth consecutive week, and it posted its largest weekly gain in three weeks: OKTA +9.76% to a 52-week high and GOOG +2.21%, crossing +1R twice, while AAPL managed +0.88% and gave back its recovery on Friday’s iPhone order-cut report. Three index records were set this week and the only index that fell was the one measuring the median company. The Russell lost 0.91% — 2.12σ, the largest reading on the board — while the S&P rose 1.15% at 1.69σ, the Dow 0.93% and the Nasdaq 0.64% at 1.01σ. In point terms: S&P +88.82, Dow +477.99, Nasdaq +175.31, Russell −25.91. A record-setting week in which small caps fell is not a rally with poor breadth; it is two different markets, and this is the third consecutive week the gap has widened.

The rotation inverted, and the week is the evidence. The Dow beat the Nasdaq over the five sessions — 0.93% against 0.64% — after a quarter in which the Nasdaq beat the Dow by more than five points. The Dow led on three of the last four sessions. That is not a one-day funding effect any more. For a book holding three long-duration growth names and nothing on the other side, it is the single most relevant structural fact of the week, and it sits oddly beside the book's own result.

The rate story turned two-sided for the first time. Monday through Wednesday it ran exactly as it had for a fortnight: ISM services prices paid up 1.4 to 74.0 against 72.9 expected, a second month above 72, while employment sat at 50.1; the two-year falling on the weak half and the ten-year making 52-week highs at 5.315% and touching 5.35% intraday, the thirty-year at 5.670%. Wednesday added the global framing — France's index down 1.2% amid mass budget protests, debt heading for 121.7% of GDP in 2027, and projected interest payments of €74.5bn exceeding what the country spends on education. The IMF's Georgieva cited record public debt; Ray Dalio warned about America's.

Then it stopped behaving. Thursday the long end eased through a thirty-year auction — the first direct test of the supply argument, and the ten-year closed near 5.24%, its lowest in a week. Friday the curve flattened: the two-year rose 3.9 basis points to 4.795% while the thirty-year sat flat at 5.608%, and it did so on a Michigan sentiment print that fell to 46.3 from 48.1 against 47.6 expected. Two consecutive sessions now fail to fit the term-premium story after five that fitted it exactly. It is not refuted — the thirty-year is still near a 24-year high and the September Fed minutes promise another hike this year — but this is the first sustained counter-evidence, and CPI on Tuesday decides it.

And the week ended with a structural repricing nobody had on the calendar. A reported $8bn SpaceX purchase of 800 MHz spectrum for Starlink Mobile took 12.26% out of T-Mobile on Friday and about 10.9% each out of Verizon and AT&T, while Crown Castle rose 11.27% and the other tower owners with it. Communication Services closed the week's worst sector. Crude went almost nowhere across five sessions — $91.11 to $90.76 — having been $87.77 on Tuesday and almost $93 on Thursday. Gold rose 0.83% to $4,174.68, its first weekly gain in three.

Nothing was opened, closed, trimmed or moved. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap (2.04R excluding the managed GOOG position), exactly where it has sat since 14 September — twenty-two sessions — because heat is set by entries, stops and sizes and none of those changed. Checked against the lowest low of all five sessions rather than any close, the nearest any holding came to a stop was AAPL at 8.88%, on Monday's 330.62. No stop was in question at any point.

The book gained $31.10 on the week and now carries +86.07 open at +4.25R — the best mark it has held. 2 of the 3 positions are above +1R, against none a fortnight ago. On $830.56 of committed capital the week was +3.74%, against the S&P's +1.15% and the Russell's −0.91%. Q3 finished at +12.31, +0.58R; Q4 has nothing realised seven sessions in, so every figure here is still open.

Friday did most of it, and on broker notes rather than company news. OKTA rose 5.41% to 232.13, a new 52-week high, on BMO Capital's move to $245 from $230 with Outperform maintained. PLTR rose 5.17% to 209.05, an all-time closing high past the $208.88 record of 3 November last year, on Goldman's upgrade to Buy from Neutral with a $230 target and Barclays initiating at Overweight with $265. Goldman's case was sovereign AI, bespoke applications, a verticalisation strategy and a head start on agents; Barclays cited deep competitive moats. Neither company said anything. That is worth stating plainly: two positions re-rated five percent in a session because analysts changed their minds, and moves made that way unwind as easily as they arrive.

GOOG rose 2.21% across the week and crossed +1R twice. It closed above the line on Wednesday at 347.37, slipped to +0.94R on Thursday when it was sold with the AI complex, and closed back above it Friday at 347.86. Three closing highs in the five sessions. The week's news was Tuesday's Constellation Energy agreement — a twenty-year, 3.6-gigawatt power deal bringing 890MW of new nuclear onto the PJM grid with over $4.3bn committed — on which Constellation rose 12.3% and Alphabet 0.22%. The supplier took the gain, which is the same split that has run through this book all month. The 28 October print is where $195-205bn of capex meets an AI funding scare.

AAPL was the week's laggard and the only holding with bad news of its own. Up 0.88% over the five sessions, which flatters it: it drifted between 330 and 334 for four days while the S&P made a record, cleared the 338.40 pre-Ternus level on Thursday for the first time since the 29 September fall, and then gave it straight back on Friday — down 1.11%, and about 2.2% premarket, on a report of iPhone 18 Pro component order cuts, with Skyworks down 6.41% on the same story. Eight sessions to recover nine dollars and one to lose four of them. Order-cut reports are a supply-chain read and are frequently wrong, but they are the first hard, checkable claim about the cycle, and the answer comes on 29 October.

What the week leaves behind. Heat at the cap, so nothing can be added. Every holding green, with OKTA at +2.46R and no stop closer than 8.9% on the week's lowest low. Two positions past the +1R threshold where a breakeven stop becomes arithmetically interesting — both flagged in the dailies, neither urgent. And a result that is entirely unrealised, in a book that has not been touched in twenty-two sessions. The honest summary of the week is that it was the best one in two months and that nothing in it was earned by a decision.

The rate thesis acquired its first counter-evidence, and the rotation inverted

1. Two sessions broke the pattern that five had built. From 29 September the long end rose on data that argued for lower yields four times in five sessions — a twelve-year low in consumer confidence, a downside core PCE miss at 3.0% against 3.3%, payrolls at 29,000 against 90,000 with 60,000 revised out, and Monday's ISM services. By Wednesday the thirty-year was at 5.671% and the ten-year had touched 5.35%, its highest since 2002, with the framing turning global. Then Thursday the long end eased through a thirty-year auction, and Friday the curve flattened on a weak sentiment print. An auction is where a supply thesis is actually tested, and that one did not go badly. This brief has published the supply argument for a fortnight; it is recording the counter-evidence with the same weight.

2. The index records and the median stock are describing different economies. The S&P set its first record since 13 August on Tuesday with genuinely broad internals — ten of eleven sectors, the equal-weight index matching the cap-weighted one, positive volume at 65.1% of NYSE turnover — and still only 24 new 52-week highs, with the McClellan Summation negative. By Friday the week showed the S&P up 1.2% and the Russell down 0.9%, and Michigan consumer sentiment had fallen to 46.3. Three records in a week when small caps fell and the consumer reached a multi-decade low of confidence is a market carried by its largest weights. This book owns three of those weights, which is why it had its largest weekly gain in three weeks.

3. The AI trade showed its first crack, and it was about funding. Thursday the Nasdaq fell 1.25% on a semiconductor sell-off while the Dow rose and most S&P constituents were higher — the first session in this run where the AI complex moved alone. The trigger was an Nvidia-backed Australian data-centre company failing to raise the support it had sought: a question about the capital behind capacity rather than about demand for compute, and the more dangerous of the two, because capacity already contracted has to be paid for regardless. Alphabet carries $195-205bn of guided capex and, since Tuesday, a twenty-year obligation for 3.6 gigawatts of power. It was the only holding to fall that day. By Friday the market had moved on; the question has not been answered.

The week the war stopped setting the price of oil

Crude ended the week where it started. WTI went $91.11 to $90.76, a move of less than four tenths of a percent across five sessions that contained a hurricane, a tanker attack and a presidential commitment on military timing. The range inside that was wide — $87.77 on Tuesday, almost $93 on Thursday — and Brent finished $103.35. A price that round-trips through that much news is a price that has stopped taking its direction from the conflict.

The most consequential thing said was about the calendar. On Thursday Trump said the United States will not attack Iran before the November midterm elections, citing productive diplomacy. It is the first dated commitment on timing since the conflict began and it removes, for roughly four weeks, the tail the oil price had been intermittently pricing. Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz happened the same day. Washington's reply to Tehran's seven-point proposal reached the cabinet through Qatari mediation on 30 September and neither side has disclosed its contents since.

What moved the price was weather and Saudi pricing. Hurricane Isaias shut in about a quarter of Gulf of Mexico output mid-week, with Chevron, Shell and BP evacuating platforms and Shell pulling off six; the premium came out on Friday as the path clarified. Against that, OPEC+ held quotas at the previous weekend and Saudi Arabia cut Arab Light for Asian buyers to $5 below benchmark, a six-year low, from a $2 discount, to take share as Gulf flows recovered. Kpler had regional exports above pre-conflict levels on 14 days in September, with a seven-day average of 18.3m barrels a day on the 30th.

And the man selling the oil spent Monday explaining that there is none spare. Aramco's Amin Nasser, at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London, called global stockpiles scarily thin: under 6 billion barrels of commercial inventory against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, less than 10% practically available, around 3 billion barrels of supply lost and over a billion drawn to cover it, with rebuilding at up to two years even after Hormuz fully reopens and an extra 2 million barrels a day needed for eighteen months. The flow has recovered and the buffer has not. That is why a storm moved crude 2.7% on Wednesday, and it is the asymmetry this book carries without being positioned for it.

September CPI on Tuesday has to settle three things at once. Whether the ISM prices indices at 77.9 in manufacturing and 74.0 in services are feeding through, when core PCE missed at 3.0% against 3.3% a fortnight ago. Whether the Fed's minutes and Waller's more hikes will likely be needed describe a committee that will act or one that is talking. And whether the long end is an inflation trade or a supply one — because Thursday's auction and Friday's flattening are the first two pieces of evidence for the second reading being wrong, and a hot print removes them.

Then nothing from the companies for a fortnight. Alphabet reports 28 October on the same day the Fed decides, Apple the 29th, Palantir 2 November, Okta in early December. Three of this book's holdings report inside five sessions at the end of the month, immediately after a rate decision. Apple's print now has an order-cut report to answer, and Alphabet's lands into a funding scare rather than an enthusiasm.

Three things to watch through the gap. Whether the broker-driven re-ratings hold: two positions in this book gained more than five percent on upgrades alone, with nothing from either company, and that is the least durable kind of gain there is. Whether the Dow keeps beating the Nasdaq — it did over a full week and on three of four sessions, and this book owns nothing on that side. And whether the Russell can stop falling: down 0.9% in a week the S&P gained 1.2% is the clearest available statement that the records are not describing the median company.

The standing discipline. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap, so nothing on the screener is actionable whatever it returns. All 3 holdings are green, the nearest any came to a stop in five sessions was 8.9% on the week's lowest low, and 2 of them now sit above +1R. Twenty-two sessions without a change — the sixth consecutive week in which the right decision was made by not being made, and the first in which that produced a result worth having.
